list.item: Using the Product Rule, we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)}{= \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {x\ln x} \right) = x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\ln x} \right) + \left( {\ln x} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)}{= x\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) + \ln x = 1 + \ln x}} \end{array}$$

Using the Quotient Rule, we obtain $$g^{\prime}(x) = \frac{x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\ln x} \right) - \left( {\ln x} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x)}{x^{2}} = \frac{x\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) - \ln x}{x^{2}} = \frac{1 - \ln x}{x^{2}}$$

note.paragraph: You can derive the formula for the derivative of $$f(x) = \ln x$$ directly from the definition of the derivative, as follows.

list.item: Put $$m = x \slash h$$ and note that $$\left. m\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. h\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . Then, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ can be written in the form $$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{m\rightarrow\infty}\ln\left( {1 + \frac{1}{m}} \right)^{m \slash x}$$

Finally, use both the fact that the natural logarithmic function is continuous and the definition of the number $$e$$ to show that $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{1}{x}\ln\left\lbrack {\lim\limits_{m\rightarrow\infty}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{m}} \right)^{m}} \right\rbrack = \frac{1}{x}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the derivative of the function $$g(t) = \ln{({t^{2}e^{- t^{2}}})}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Here again, to save a lot of work, we first simplify the given expression using the properties of logarithms. We have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{g(t)}{= \ln{({t^{2}e^{- t^{2}}})}}} \\ {\phantom{g(t)}{= \ln t^{2} + \ln e^{- t^{2}}} {\ln mn = \ln m + \ln n}} \\ {\phantom{g(t)}{= 2\ln t - t^{2}} {\ln m^{n} = n\ln m \text{and} \ln e = 1}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Logarithmic Differentiation
section.paragraph: As we saw in Examples 3 and 4, the task of finding the derivative of a given function can sometimes be made easier by first applying the laws of logarithms to simplify the function. We now illustrate a process called logarithmic differentiation , which not only simplifies the calculation of the derivatives of certain functions but also enables us to compute the derivatives of functions that we could not otherwise differentiate using the techniques developed thus far.
